meeting_header: Date: 2027-06-03 | Start: 15:30 UTC | Duration: 52m | Redwood: Maya Chen, Diego Alvarez | Petrichor: Anika Rao, Jonas Meyer, Priya Singh
summary: Security review focused on encryption in transit (TLS/mTLS) and at rest (KMS/BYOK/HSM). Discussed Redwood integration patterns for BYOK, HSM attestation, key rotation/escrow, audit logging, and data residency implications. Agreed to share detailed integration diagrams, SOC 2 evidence, and run a PoC for BYOK handshake and TLS mutual auth. Action items assigned for docs and timeline.
topics: Audit logs and retention for compliance
Data residency and regional key separation
Key rotation, emergency revocation, and forensics
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Okay good afternoon everyone, thanks for making time. Quick intro, I'm Maya, AE on the Petrichor account, with Diego from our SE team.
[00:22] Anika (Petrichor): Hi Maya, thanks. I'm Anika, Head of Security. On the call we also have Jonas and Priya.
[00:32] Diego (Redwood SE): Hi all, Diego here. We'll go through how Redwood handles TLS, KMS integrations, BYOK/HSM options, and then map to your auditing needs.
[00:45] Jonas (Petrichor): Great. High level — we need to confirm that data in transit is authenticated and that keys used for at-rest encryption can be customer-managed. Also auditors want proof of key custody separation.
[01:10] Priya (Petrichor): And timeline for the pilot — we need to show this to internal compliance next week, so any materials you can share fast would help.
[01:25] Maya: Absolutely. We'll share SOC 2 artifacts and an integration diagram. First question to you: where are your current keys stored? Cloud KMS? On-prem HSM?
[01:40] Anika: We run AWS KMS for most services but we also have a Thales HSM for the most sensitive workloads. We want BYOK for Redwood, ideally with HSM-backed wrapping keys.
[02:05] Diego: That aligns with what we support. Redwood can integrate with customer KMS via external key wrap — we call it BYOK/HSM flow — where you import an encrypted model key and Redwood never sees the plaintext.
[02:27] Jonas: So you never have the unwrapped root? How does rotation work then?
[02:35] Diego: Correct, we never persist plaintext. Rotation happens via re-wrapping: customer rotates master CMK in their KMS/HSM and re-wraps the customer wrapping key used for objects. We support staged rollouts so in-flight tokens aren't impacted.
[02:56] Anika: Can you walk through an actual handshake? For example, our compliance requires mTLS and an auditable key exchange log.
[03:12] Diego: Yes. Two parts: transport (TLS/mTLS) and storage (KMS wrap). For TLS we recommend mutual TLS between your VPC endpoint and the Redwood private egress. You present a client cert, we validate CN and SAN. We also capture handshake metadata in our audit pipeline — time, cipher suite, client cert thumbprint. Logs are forwarded to the audit log sink you specify.
[03:44] Maya: Note that some transcription systems render thumbprint as "thumbprint" but it's the SHA-256 fingerprint we record — that's what auditors typically look for.
[03:57] Anika: Good. About HSM attestation: auditors ask for an HSM attestation report showing that the key wrap happened in an HSM. Does Redwood provide any attestation or do we need to provide that from our vendor?
[04:14] Diego: Redwood does not operate your HSM. The attestation comes from your HSM vendor (e.g., Thales, AWS Nitro enclave attestation/CloudHSM signing). However, Redwood will record the attestation token you present during onboarding and include its hash in our audit logs — effectively binding the attestation to the provisioning event.
[04:36] Priya: So we upload the attestation, it gets hashed and put into the access ledger for later verification?
[04:44] Diego: Exactly. The attestation blob remains your artifact; we only store its SHA-256 and associated metadata.
[04:53] [05:00] Jonas: How about emergency key revocation or compromise — say a key is suspected compromised, what's the failover?
[05:08] Maya: Good question. There are two lanes: immediate revocation of the CMK in your KMS which prevents new unwrap operations, and a Redwood side policy to reject tokens signed with that key ID. For in-flight data, we can trigger a re-encrypt job or require clients to re-authenticate. We normally recommend a documented runbook — we'll share our template.
[05:34] Anika: We need that re-encrypt path to be auditable and included in our incident response.
[05:40] Diego: Our platform emits events for key lifecycle operations: wrap, unwrap attempt, rotation, revocation. Each event includes key ID, actor, timestamp, request ID, and result code. Those go to your audit sink with configurable retention.
[06:02] [06:30] Jonas: About data residency: we have EMEA customers that require keys to be generated and stored in eu-west-1 KMS. Can we have per-region key separation?
[06:40] Diego: Yes. Redwood supports region-scoped key policies. You can provision a separate CMK per region and we route key unwrap operations to the region where the encrypted blob is stored. That satisfies residency and reduces cross-border transfer.
[06:59] Priya: Do you support key hierarchy? Like a regional master that wraps per-tenant keys?
[07:07] Diego: Yes, hierarchical wrapping is supported. Typical pattern: HSM-backed root CMK -> regional intermediate keys -> workload keys. We store only the wrapped keys and metadata.
[07:20] Anika: Auditors also ask for separation of duties — who in Redwood can trigger unwraps? We need least privilege.
[07:29] Maya: By default, only the runtime agents have the ability to call unwrap. In Dedicated/Private deployments you can enforce stricter RBAC; for hosted customers we have role-based controls and audit trails. We can provide a list of roles and their privileges.
[07:45] Diego: Also note there are operator-level safeguards: unwrap operations require a signed request token and we support token scoping by route and purpose.
[07:56] [08:20] Anika: On TLS: do you support pinned ciphers or will Redwood negotiate? Our compliance wants TLS 1.3 only and specific AEAD suites.
[08:30] Diego: We default to TLS 1.3. You can require cipher suites and we can pin to a restricted list (e.g., TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256). We'll surface that in the mTLS config.
[08:43] Jonas: What about TLS termination in the platform? If we use Redwood hosted, where is TLS terminated?
[08:50] Maya: For hosted API, TLS is terminated at our edge; we then use an internal mTLS channel to the runtime. For private deployments, TLS termination can be customer-controlled in the VPC. That's why many enterprises choose Dedicated or Private for strict termination policies.
[09:06] Priya: We might prefer a private instance for our EU customers. Can Redwood's private control plane still use our BYOK?
[09:15] Diego: Yes, Private supports direct HSM/KMS integration inside your VPC, and keys never leave your network. We can support HSM connectors and local KMS proxies.
[09:28] [09:45] Anika: A few auditors ask for end-to-end proof that the service never had plaintext. Do you provide a signed certificate or audit bundle proving that flows were all wrapped/unwrapped under client control?
[09:58] Diego: We provide an audit bundle: sequence of signed events with request IDs, key ID references, and hashes of wrapped payloads. We can sign the bundle with our platform key and you can cross-check the chain with your HSM signature. It's not a formal cryptographic attestation of 'never saw plaintext', but combined with HSM attestation and event hashes it's usually sufficient for auditors.
[10:32] Maya: I'll note that wording must be careful in documentation — we don't want to promise absolute impossibility but provide evidence.
[10:39] [11:00] Jonas: On rotation: what's the impact to cached KV state? Our KV cache is used heavily for low-latency inference.
[11:10] Diego: We discussed this: rotation is ideally off-peak. For KV caches, we support wrap versioning — tokens include a wrap key version so the runtime can accept multiple versions during a grace period. After we confirm no active references to the old version, you can expire it.
[11:30] Priya: How long is the grace window?
[11:35] Diego: Configurable; common values are 24-72 hours depending on workload. We recommend 48 hours for inference workloads to balance risk and operational ease.
[11:50] [12:00] Anika: Auditing retention — we need logs for 7 years for certain regs. Can Redwood forward to our long-term archive?
[12:08] Maya: Yes, logs can be forwarded to your S3/GCS archive or to your SIEM. We also support log shippers like Fluentd. Retention is a customer policy when logs are in your account; for hosted retention options we can negotiate extended retention as an add-on.
[12:30] Jonas: Is the audit log tamper-evident? We need WORM-like properties sometimes.
[12:36] Diego: For tamper-evidence, we recommend streaming to a write-once storage or using an append-only ledger. Redwood can emit a daily signed digest — a hash chain — that you can anchor in your own ledger.
[12:52] [13:10] Priya: About consent and PII: if inference outputs contain PII stored in model caches, is that encrypted under the same keys?
[13:20] Diego: Yes, everything at rest in Redwood storage is encrypted under customer keys where BYOK is configured. Ephemeral caches may be different; for sensitive PII we recommend workload-level encryption and reduced cache TTLs.
[13:36] Anika: We'll need to map where PII might touch caches and set policies.
[13:42] Maya: We can run a data flow mapping session as a follow-on.
[13:48] [14:10] Jonas: Let's talk about proof-of-concept: we want to test a BYOK unwrap flow and mTLS handshake with our Thales HSM. What does Redwood need?
[14:22] Diego: We need an onboarding package: HSM attestation blob, a test CMK wrapped key blob, test cert for mTLS, and a small sample payload. We can provide shell scripts and a small harness to perform unwraps and verify audit events.
[14:40] Priya: Are there network requirements? We have strict egress rules.
[14:46] Diego: For Private/Dedicated, we can work through VPC peering or private endpoints. For hosted POC we can also set up a temporary VPN or allowlisted IPs. We'll document the ports (443 for TLS, optional port for HSM connector) and IP blocks.
[15:02] [15:30] Anika: One more — key escrow. Some regs ask for an escrow to recover data if keys are lost. Do you support vetted escrow mechanisms?
[15:40] Diego: We support escrow patterns but we don't operate an escrow service. Typical approach: you escrow to a third-party vault or to a multi-sig escrow service. Redwood can store an encrypted copy of wrapping metadata but not the escrowed plaintext key. We can also integrate with your chosen escrow vendor's API as part of onboarding.
[16:03] Maya: We'll include a few reference escrow vendors and playbooks in the packet.
[16:12] [16:45] Jonas: About certifications: can you provide SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 evidence for the hosted control plane?
[16:55] Maya: Yes, we'll share SOC 2 Type II report excerpts and ISO 27001 scope. For Dedicated/Private we provide evidence for the parts we operate; we also document the customer-controlled portions that fall out of scope.
[17:12] Priya: For our auditors, we may need a joint responsibility matrix.
[17:18] Maya: We'll produce that as well — control mapping between Petrichor and Redwood.
[17:24] [17:50] Anika: A minor point: can we restrict which Redwood engineers can view audit logs or unblock keys? We need separation and approvals.
[18:00] Diego: Yes, RBAC is granular. You can create roles with read-only audit access, roles for key lifecycle requests that require multiple approvers, and we support SSO/SAML for provisioning. We can also integrate with your PAM for escalations.
[18:18] Jonas: Does Redwood store any long-lived secrets for customers?
[18:22] Maya: We store wrapped keys and metadata only, not plaintext secrets. Long-lived secrets like service account keys are provisioned per onboarding and can be rotated or revoked by you.
[18:34] [19:00] Anika: A couple of transcription notes from our side: you mentioned "wrap versioning" earlier, we want that spelled out in the doc with examples.
[19:08] Diego: Will do, I'll include an example sequence: v1 -> v2 grace window -> retire v1.
[19:15] Priya: For the audit bundle, do you include raw TLS handshake logs or just metadata?
[19:22] Diego: We include metadata by default (thumbprints, cipher, time). Raw PCAP-level captures are heavier and only for agreed-forensics or PoC with explicit retention and access controls — we can support that on request.
[19:37] [20:00] Maya: Ok, let's capture next steps — I've already noted key items, but to recap: we'll send SOC 2 + ISO artifacts, Diego will send TLS checklist and PoC scripts, and Petrichor will provide HSM attestation and test artifacts.
[20:16] Anika: Sounds good. Any blockers on Redwood's side?
[20:20] Diego: No blockers. We'll need the attestation blob and network access details to start the PoC.
[20:28] Jonas: Expected timeline? We want results before our compliance review on 2027-06-21.
[20:34] Maya: We can aim for PoC run 2027-06-14 to 06-18 and deliver findings by 06-20. That meets your review date.
[20:46] [21:10] Priya: One last quick question about encryption algorithms: do you support customers requiring RSA-based key wrapping or is it all AES-KW and RSA-OAEP?
[21:20] Diego: We support AES-KW, RSA-OAEP, and KMS vendor-specific schemes. For HSMs you'll often use RSA-OAEP or vendor-wrapped schemes. We'll include supported algorithms in the design doc.
[21:36] Anika: Thanks. That addresses the technical side.
[21:40] Maya: Great. We'll follow up with the packet by end of day tomorrow.
[21:48] [22:05] Jonas: Appreciate it, we'll assemble the attestation artifacts and the list of regulators.
[22:12] Anika: Thanks all.
[22:15] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll send the calendar invite for the PoC kickoff.
[22:20] [22:30] Diego: Bye.
[22:33] Speaker 1: (muted) bye.
[22:40] [END]
